title: David Made King and His Mighty Men
summary: All Israel comes to David at Hebron, recalls God's word that he would shepherd the people, and anoints him king. David captures the Jebusite fortress of Zion, which becomes the City of David, and grows greater because the LORD of Hosts is with him. The chapter then lists the chiefs of his mighty men and their exploits, including three who risked their lives to bring him water from Bethlehem, which he poured out to the LORD.
story: Saul is dead and the LORD has turned the kingdom to David (10:14). The Chronicler moves directly to all Israel gathering at Hebron to make David king. He passes over the seven years in which David ruled only Judah while Saul's son Esh-baal ruled the north, and the civil war between them (2 Samuel 2 to 4). In Chronicles the whole nation comes at once, united, recognizing what God has said. Then comes Jerusalem: the city that will be the home of the ark and the site of the temple is taken in the first act of David's reign. The list of mighty men, which 2 Samuel places near the end of David's life, is set here at the beginning, to show that David's kingdom was built and strengthened by a great company of loyal followers from across Israel.
historical:
Verses 1 to 9 follow 2 Samuel 5:1-10, and verses 10 to 41 (through Uriah the Hittite) follow 2 Samuel 23:8-39, while the names from Zabad son of Ahlai (verse 41) to the end of the chapter are added from another source. David is usually dated around 1010 to 970 BC, and his capture of Jerusalem shortly after he became king over all Israel is commonly placed around 1000 BC. Jerusalem (Jebus) was a Canaanite city held by the Jebusites, set on a narrow ridge with steep valleys on three sides and a spring (the Gihon) at its foot, which made it strong and easy to defend. It also lay between Judah and the northern tribes and had belonged to none of them, which made it a politically neutral capital.

The supporting terraces of verse 8 translate the Hebrew Millo, probably a system of terraces or earthworks. Archaeologists working in the City of David have uncovered a large stepped stone structure on the eastern slope, which some identify with the Millo or with David's building work, though its date and purpose are debated. The Cave of Adullam, the Valley of Rephaim, and Bethlehem locate the water episode in Judah's hill country during David's wars with the Philistines, before or soon after he became king.
cultural:
When the tribes say to David, “Here we are, your own flesh and blood” (verse 1), they are claiming kinship, which in the ancient world was the basis of loyalty and obligation. The covenant David made with the elders (verse 3) was a formal agreement setting out the relationship between king and people before the LORD. Anointing with oil marked a person as set apart for a task by God. The image of the king as a shepherd was common across the ancient Near East, where rulers claimed to shepherd their peoples, but in Israel it carried the added sense that the flock belonged to God.

The mighty men were an elite corps of warriors, organized into ranks: the Three, the Thirty, and their commanders. Their exploits were recorded as a roll of honor. Several of them were foreigners, including Zelek the Ammonite, Ithmah the Moabite, and Uriah the Hittite (verse 41), a sign that loyalty to David could cross ethnic lines. David's pouring out of the water was a drink offering. In Israel's law blood belonged to God and was not to be consumed (Leviticus 17:10-14), and David treats water won at the risk of lives as if it were their blood, too precious to drink and fit only to be given to God.
literary: The chapter has two parts: the enthronement and capture of Jerusalem (verses 1 to 9), and the roll of mighty men (verses 10 to 47). The first part is framed by the phrase all Israel and ends with a theological summary: David became greater and greater, because the LORD of Hosts was with him (verse 9). Verse 10 connects the two parts: the mighty men, together with all Israel, strengthened his kingdom according to the word of the LORD. The roll moves from narratives about the leading warriors (verses 11 to 25) to a bare list of names (verses 26 to 47). The account of Eleazar in verses 12 to 14 appears to combine the stories of two warriors, Eleazar and Shammah, found separately in 2 Samuel 23:9-12; many scholars think a copyist's eye skipped from one mention of the Philistines gathering to another, dropping the lines between.

outline.t: All Israel anoints David king at Hebron
David captures Jerusalem and grows greater
The chiefs of the mighty men: Jashobeam and Eleazar
Water from the well of Bethlehem
The roll of David's mighty men

doctrines.note: David becomes king according to the word of the LORD through Samuel (verse 3), and the kingdom is strengthened according to that word (verse 10). The Chronicler presents David's kingship as God's appointment, not a seizure of power.
David makes a covenant with the elders before the LORD. The king is bound to the people and both are bound to God. Israel's kingship was meant to be accountable, not absolute.
David grew greater and greater because the LORD of Hosts was with him. His success is credited to God's presence, not merely to his skill or his warriors.

words.note: Raah, to shepherd or pasture. God's word to David was that he would shepherd God's people (verse 2). The king's first task is care for the flock, not power over it. The same verb describes God as the shepherd of Israel in Psalm 80:1 and Ezekiel 34.
Nagid, leader or ruler, a word often used for one designated by God to lead. It stresses appointment by God rather than hereditary right, and Chronicles uses it for David and later for Solomon.
Mashach, to anoint. The elders anointed David king (verse 3). From this verb comes mashiach, anointed one, the word behind Messiah. To be anointed was to be marked and set apart by God for a task.

Dam, blood. David calls the water the blood of the men who risked their lives (verse 19). In Israel's law blood belonged to God as the seat of life, and David's act treats his men's courage as a sacred offering.

christ: Several threads in this chapter run toward Jesus. David is anointed (mashach) to shepherd God's people; the word anointed gives us Messiah, and the New Testament proclaims Jesus as the anointed son of David. God's promise that David would shepherd his people is echoed in Ezekiel 34:23, which looks forward to a shepherd from David's line, and Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). The water episode also offers a striking contrast. David refused to drink water bought with his men's lives and poured it out to God. Jesus, the greater son of David, did not ask his followers to risk their lives for him first; he gave his own life for them, and at the Last Supper he gave the cup as his blood poured out for many (Mark 14:24). These are thematic links, not predictions in the chapter.

hard.q: Why does Chronicles leave out the civil war, David's years ruling Judah alone, and other parts of Samuel's account?
hard.a: The Chronicler omits David's seven years in Hebron as king of Judah only, his war with Saul's house, and later his adultery with Bathsheba and Absalom's rebellion. Some critics have seen this as idealization or even whitewashing. Most scholars now read it differently. The Chronicler's readers already had the books of Samuel and Kings; he was not hiding what everyone knew. He selected and arranged material to make his own points for his own generation: that David was the king God chose, that all Israel was united under him, and that his reign centered on preparing for God's house. He even mentions the seven years in Hebron in passing (3:4 and 29:27), and he includes Uriah the Hittite among the mighty men (11:41), a name his readers would recognize. Chronicles is best read alongside Samuel and Kings, as a second portrait painted from a different angle, rather than as a replacement for them.

questions: God's word to David was that he would shepherd God's people. What would it look like for you to lead in your home, work, or church as a shepherd rather than a ruler?
David refused to drink water his men had risked their lives for and poured it out to God. What in your life has been bought at great cost by others, and how do you honor it?
The mighty men included foreigners from nations that were Israel's enemies. What does their loyalty to David suggest about who belongs among God's people?
